source.text: Οἱ οὖν Ἰουδαῖοι, ἐπεὶ παρασκευὴ ἦν, ἵνα μὴ μείνῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὰ σώματα ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ, ἦν γὰρ μεγάλη ἡ ἡμέρα ἐκείνου τοῦ σαββάτου, ἠρώτησαν τὸν Πιλᾶτον ἵνα κατεαγῶσιν αὐτῶν τὰ σκέλη καὶ ἀρθῶσιν.

records.literal_gloss: The therefore Jews, since Preparation it was, so that not might remain on the cross the bodies on the Sabbath, was for great the day of that the Sabbath, asked the Pilate that might be broken of them the legs and they might be taken away.

en.L: So the Jews, since it was [the] Preparation, so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for the day of that Sabbath was a great [one]), asked Pilate that their legs be broken and [that] they be taken away.
en.B: It was the day of Preparation, and the Jewish leaders did not want the bodies to stay on the crosses over the Sabbath, because that Sabbath was a day of special importance. So they asked Pilate to have the men's legs broken and the bodies removed.
en.R: It was the day of Preparation, when people got everything ready for the Sabbath. The Jewish leaders did not want the bodies left on the crosses on the Sabbath, because that Sabbath was a very special day. So they asked Pilate to have the legs of the men broken, so that they would die sooner, and to have the bodies taken down.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the authorities, the chief priests and those with them
decisions.reason: They act as a body and make a formal request of the Roman governor, as the chief priests and their officers did throughout the trial (18:28-31; 19:6-7, 12, 15, 21). It is not the people as a whole: Jesus, his disciples, and Joseph and Nicodemus, who bury him, are Jews.

decisions.choice: Preparation: the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday
alternatives: the day before the Passover only
decisions.reason: The word means preparation, and it was the ordinary name for the sixth day of the week, when food was cooked and everything made ready so that no work need be done on the Sabbath (Mark 15:42 calls it "the day before the Sabbath"). John has called this day "the Preparation of the Passover" (19:14); in his account the Passover meal was still to be eaten that evening (18:28). The Sabbath began at sunset, so the time was short.

decisions.choice: so that the bodies would not remain on the cross: to keep the law about the body of an executed man
decisions.reason: The law said that the body of a man hanged on a tree must not stay there overnight but must be buried the same day, so as not to defile the land (Deuteronomy 21:22-23; compare Joshua 8:29; 10:26-27). The coming Sabbath made the matter more pressing. The Romans often left the crucified on their crosses for days; the request asks the governor to set that aside. "The cross" is singular in the Greek but speaks of each cross: three men were crucified (19:18).

decisions.choice: a great day: that Sabbath was also a feast day of Passover week
alternatives: only that every Sabbath was holy
decisions.reason: John has said that the Passover meal was to be eaten that evening (18:28; 19:14), so the Sabbath that followed was also the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, a day of holy assembly (Leviticus 23:6-7). A Sabbath that fell on a feast day was doubly holy. The Greek says literally "great was the day of that Sabbath".

decisions.choice: that their legs be broken and they be taken away: to bring death sooner, so that the bodies could be taken down before the Sabbath
decisions.reason: Breaking the legs of the crucified was a known Roman practice. A crucified man with broken legs could no longer push himself up to breathe, and so he died soon after. "Taken away" means removed from the cross for burial; the same verb is used of Joseph taking the body in verse 38.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: It was the day of Preparation ... because that Sabbath was a day of special importance (B); a very special day (R)
alternatives: since it was Preparation ... (for the day of that Sabbath was great) (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable begin with the time and keep the reasons in order without the Greek's long, interrupted sentence. "A great day" would not tell a modern reader that the day was especially holy (meaning decision m4); "high day" is old-fashioned. Balanced and Readable say "crosses" because there were three (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: when people got everything ready for the Sabbath; so that they would die sooner
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the day of Preparation was (meaning decision m2) and why the legs were broken (meaning decision m5), which a young reader would not know. It adds nothing about suffering that the text does not say.

source.text: ἦλθον οὖν οἱ στρατιῶται, καὶ τοῦ μὲν πρώτου κατέαξαν τὰ σκέλη καὶ τοῦ ἄλλου τοῦ συσταυρωθέντος αὐτῷ·

records.literal_gloss: Came therefore the soldiers, and of the on one hand first they broke the legs and of the other the [one] having been crucified with him;

en.L: So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}};
en.B: So the soldiers came. They broke the first man's legs, and then the legs of the other man crucified with Jesus.
en.R: So the soldiers came. First they broke one man's legs, and then the other man's legs. Both men had been crucified with Jesus.

decisions.choice: so the soldiers came: Pilate granted the request
decisions.reason: John does not say in words that Pilate agreed, but "so" (therefore) shows that the soldiers acted on the request of verse 31. The soldiers are the Roman squad that crucified Jesus (19:23); the sentence is carried out by Rome's men under Rome's governor.

decisions.choice: the first and the other: the two men crucified on either side of Jesus
decisions.reason: These are the two men of 19:18, crucified "one on each side, and Jesus in the middle". The paired words "the first ... the other" suggest that the soldiers came to one, then the other, and to Jesus last (verse 33); John does not explain the order.

decisions.choice: the first man, the other man (R); Jesus (for "him")
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "man" where the Greek has only "the first" and "the other", and name Jesus for "him", so that the reader can follow who is meant. Literal keeps the pronoun, with the deity pronoun setting.

source.text: ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐλθόντες, ὡς εἶδον ἤδη αὐτὸν τεθνηκότα, οὐ κατέαξαν αὐτοῦ τὰ σκέλη, ἀλλ’ εἷς τῶν στρατιωτῶν λόγχῃ αὐτοῦ τὴν πλευρὰν ἔνυξεν, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν εὐθὺς αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ.

records.literal_gloss: But to the Jesus having come, when they saw already him having died, not they broke of him the legs, \v 34 but one of the soldiers with a spear of him the side pierced, and came out immediately blood and water.

en.L: But having come to Jesus, when they saw that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was already dead, they did not break {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} legs, \v 34 but one of the soldiers pierced {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
en.B: But when they reached Jesus, they saw that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had already died. So they did not break {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} legs. \v 34 One of the soldiers, however, drove a spear into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} side, and at once blood and water flowed out.
en.R: But when they came to Jesus, they saw that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was already dead. So they did not break {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} legs. \v 34 But a soldier pushed a spear into {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} side. Right away blood and water came out.

decisions.choice: already dead: he had died before they reached him
decisions.reason: The verb is in the perfect: he was already in the state of death. John has told of the moment of death in 19:30, when Jesus bowed his head and gave up his spirit. The soldiers, whose task it was to see that the condemned died, find him dead; Mark 15:44-45 likewise tells of Pilate checking that Jesus was dead.

decisions.choice: pierced his side with a spear: a thrust of the spear into the body
decisions.reason: The verb can mean anything from a prod to a deep stab; here what follows, and Thomas's words about putting his hand into Jesus's side (20:25, 27), show a real wound. John does not say why the soldier did it, perhaps to make certain of the death. The verb is not the one in the quotation of verse 37, but John sees this act as fulfilling it.

decisions.choice: blood and water came out: first of all a plain fact, showing a real death of a real body; any further meaning is left unstated
alternatives: a sign of the Spirit, the living water that flows from Jesus once he is glorified (7:38-39)
a sign of the water and blood of 1 John 5:6-8
a sign of the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper
decisions.reason: John does not explain the blood and water; he stresses instead that it was seen and testified to (verse 35). At the least it shows that Jesus truly died as a human being, with a body of flesh and blood (1:14; compare 1 John 4:2-3). Readers have long seen more in it: in this Gospel water stands for the Spirit and the life Jesus gives (4:14; 7:38-39), and blood for the life he lays down (6:53-56). These links are possible but not stated, so they are left to the footnote; the text itself gives no medical account.

decisions.choice: drove a spear into his side, at once (B); pushed a spear into his side, right away (R)
alternatives: pierced his side with a spear (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what the soldier did (meaning decision m2) without adding detail. Literal keeps "pierced".

decisions.choice: separate sentences: ... So they did not break his legs. One of the soldiers, however (B); But a soldier (R) ...
decisions.reason: The Greek runs on in one sentence with participles; Balanced and Readable break it where verse 34 begins and keep the contrast "not ... but".

source.text: καὶ ὁ ἑωρακὼς μεμαρτύρηκεν, καὶ ἀληθινὴ αὐτοῦ ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία, καὶ ἐκεῖνος οἶδεν ὅτι ἀληθῆ λέγει, ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς πιστεύητε.

records.literal_gloss: And the [one] having seen has testified, and true of him is the testimony, and that one knows that true things he says, so that also you may believe.

en.L: And the one who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true, and that one knows that he is saying true things, so that you also may believe.
en.B: The one who saw this has testified to it, and his testimony is true. He knows that what he says is true, and he has told it so that you also may believe.
en.R: The man who saw this has told about it, and what he says can be trusted. He knows that he is telling the truth. He has told it so that you also will believe.

decisions.choice: the one who has seen: an eyewitness at the cross, most likely the disciple whom Jesus loved
alternatives: an unnamed witness other than the beloved disciple
decisions.reason: John does not name him. The disciple whom Jesus loved stood at the cross (19:26-27), and at the end of the Gospel the same disciple is said to be the one "who testifies to these things and wrote them" (21:24), so he is most likely meant. The perfect tenses ("has seen", "has testified") present the testimony as given and still standing.

decisions.choice: that one knows: the eyewitness himself, who knows that he speaks the truth
alternatives: Christ, or God, who knows that the witness speaks the truth (a solemn appeal to a higher witness)
the writer of the Gospel, speaking of the eyewitness as someone else
decisions.reason: The word is the pointing pronoun "that one", not a simple "he". John often uses it to refer back to the person just named (1:8; 9:9, 11, 36-37), and the natural reading is that the eyewitness himself is sure of what he says. Because the pronoun can point away from the speaker, some take it of Christ, who is called "that one" in 1 John 2:6 and 3:3-7, or of God, called on as a witness to the testimony. The text does not settle it, so all levels keep a plain pronoun.

decisions.choice: true ... true things: his testimony is genuine, and what he says is true
decisions.reason: Two related words are used. The first, used of the testimony, means true in the sense of genuine and reliable, the word of "the true light" (1:9) and "the true vine" (15:1). The second, "true things", means that what he says is in accord with the facts. Together they stress that the account can be relied on; under the law, testimony was weighed by its witnesses (8:17; Deuteronomy 19:15).

decisions.choice: so that you also may believe: a verb form that suggests going on in belief (SBLGNT)
alternatives: "so that you also may come to believe" (many manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has a present form of the verb, read in some early manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) and Codex Vaticanus; many other manuscripts have the aorist, which can suggest coming to belief. The same split occurs at 20:31, where the Gospel states its purpose in the same words. The difference is slight, and both readings say that the testimony is given for the reader's belief, so there is no footnote. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: you also: the readers of the Gospel
decisions.reason: John turns from the story to address the readers directly, as he does again at 20:31. "You" is plural. The purpose of the testimony is not only that the facts be known but that the readers believe.

decisions.choice: testified, testimony (L, B); told about it, what he says can be trusted (R); that one (L); He (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Testify" and "testimony", as elsewhere in John (1:7; 3:11; 5:32; 8:13-14). Readable uses everyday words for the same ideas. Literal keeps "that one"; Balanced and Readable use a plain "He", which leaves the reference open as the Greek does (meaning decision m2). No pronoun here takes the deity pronoun setting, since the default reading takes it of the eyewitness.

source.text: ἐγένετο γὰρ ταῦτα ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ· Ὀστοῦν οὐ συντριβήσεται αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Happened for these things so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "A bone not will be broken of him."

en.L: For these things happened so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not a bone of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will be broken."
en.B: These things took place so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: "Not one bone of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} will be broken."
en.R: These things happened to make what the Scripture says come true: "None of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} bones will be broken."

decisions.choice: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12), and the righteous man whom God protects (Psalm 34:21)
decisions.reason: The law of the Passover says that no bone of the lamb is to be broken (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). Psalm 34:21 (verse 20 where the title is not counted) says that the LORD keeps all the bones of the righteous man, so that not one of them is broken. John's wording, with the future passive "will be broken", is closest to the psalm in its Greek translation; the theme of the Passover runs through his account. Jesus is "the Lamb of God" (1:29, 36) and dies on the day of Preparation for the Passover (19:14), so both passages are probably in view. The footnote gives the references.

decisions.choice: these things: what happened in verses 32-34
alternatives: only the not breaking of his legs
decisions.reason: "These things" covers the soldiers leaving his legs unbroken and the spear thrust, since verse 37 gives a second Scripture for the piercing. "For" ties the two quotations to the testimony of verse 35: what the witness saw is what Scripture had said.

decisions.choice: so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: the events happened as God's purpose, written in Scripture, required
decisions.reason: John uses the same words of the events of the passion at 13:18; 15:25; 17:12 and 19:24, 28. He does not mean that the soldiers set out to fulfill Scripture; they did not know it. What they did by chance and by order happened within God's purpose.

decisions.choice: Not one bone of his (B); None of his bones (R); to make what the Scripture says come true (R)
alternatives: A bone of him will not be broken
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the stress where the Greek puts it, on "not a bone". Readable gives the sense of "fulfilled" in plain words, as at 13:18.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} (L); {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: In the books of Moses the words are about the Passover lamb, and in the psalm about the righteous man; John applies them to Jesus, so the pronoun takes the deity pronoun setting, as in other quotations applied to him (2:17).

source.text: καὶ πάλιν ἑτέρα γραφὴ λέγει· Ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν.

records.literal_gloss: And again another Scripture says: "They will look at [him] whom they pierced."

en.L: And again another Scripture says, "They will look at [the one] whom they pierced."
en.B: And another passage of Scripture also says, "They will look at the one they pierced."
en.R: And another place in the Scripture says, "They will look at the one they pierced."

decisions.choice: Zechariah 12:10, in a wording close to the Hebrew
decisions.reason: In Zechariah 12:10 the LORD promises to pour out a spirit of grace and pleading on the house of David and the people of Jerusalem: they will look to him whom they pierced and will mourn for him as for an only son. In the Hebrew the LORD speaks, saying "they will look to me", so in some sense the one pierced is identified with God himself. The usual Greek translation of Zechariah reads differently here, and John's wording is closer to the Hebrew. Reviewers should check the wording against the Greek and Hebrew of Zechariah.

decisions.choice: they will look: those who pierced him will see him; the prophecy may also look beyond the cross
alternatives: only the soldiers and onlookers at the cross
only a future seeing at his coming (Revelation 1:7)
decisions.reason: Those at the cross saw the one whom they had pierced. In Zechariah the looking leads to mourning and repentance, and Revelation 1:7 uses the same verse of his coming, when "every eye will see him, even those who pierced him". John may also have in mind the looking in faith of 3:14-15 and 12:32. The text leaves this open.

decisions.choice: again another Scripture: a second passage adds its witness
decisions.reason: "Again" introduces a further quotation, as at 12:39 and in Hebrews 1:5-6; it does not mean that the same thing happened a second time. Two Scriptures, one for the unbroken bones and one for the piercing, match the two things the witness saw.

decisions.choice: [the one] (L); the one (B, R); another passage of Scripture also (B); another place in the Scripture (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "whom"; Literal brackets "the one" and the other levels say it. No deity pronoun is needed. "Another Scripture" means another passage, and Balanced and Readable say so; Balanced gives the sense of "again" with "also" (meaning decision m3).

source.text: Μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ἠρώτησεν τὸν Πιλᾶτον Ἰωσὴφ ἀπὸ Ἁριμαθαίας, ὢν μαθητὴς τοῦ Ἰησοῦ κεκρυμμένος δὲ διὰ τὸν φόβον τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ· καὶ ἐπέτρεψεν ὁ Πιλᾶτος.

records.literal_gloss: After but these things asked the Pilate Joseph from Arimathea, being a disciple of the Jesus but having been hidden because of the fear of the Jews, that he might take away the body of the Jesus; and permitted the Pilate.

en.L: Now after these things Joseph from Arimathea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly because of the fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus; and Pilate gave permission.
en.B: After this, Joseph of Arimathea, a disciple of Jesus who had kept it hidden because he feared the Jewish leaders, asked Pilate for permission to take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate granted it.
en.R: After this, a man named Joseph, from the town of Arimathea, asked Pilate to let him take away the body of Jesus. Joseph was a disciple of Jesus. But he had kept that a secret, because he was afraid of the Jewish leaders. Pilate said that he could take the body.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the authorities
decisions.reason: Joseph was himself a Jew, and the other Gospels say he was a member of the council (Mark 15:43; Luke 23:50-51). What he feared was the leaders who had condemned Jesus, as in 7:13; 9:22; 12:42 and 20:19, not his own people.

decisions.choice: Joseph of Arimathea: a man of standing who had not openly followed Jesus
decisions.reason: John says only that he was a secret disciple. The other Gospels add that he was rich (Matthew 27:57), a respected member of the council who was waiting for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43), and that he had not agreed with the council's decision (Luke 23:51). Luke calls Arimathea a town of the Judeans; its site is not certain.

decisions.choice: secretly because of fear: he had kept his discipleship hidden
decisions.reason: The word is a perfect participle, "having been hidden": he had been a disciple in secret until now. John has spoken of rulers who believed in Jesus but did not say so for fear of being put out of the synagogue (12:42-43). By asking for the body, Joseph now acts in the open.

decisions.choice: asked Pilate for the body: the body of an executed man was at the governor's disposal
decisions.reason: A man executed by Rome could be refused burial, or his body could be given to those who asked for it; it was the governor's decision. Pilate grants the request. The same verb, "take away", was used in the request of verse 31.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: a disciple of Jesus who had kept it hidden (B); separate sentences and "from the town of Arimathea" (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the description inside the sentence, as the Greek does. Readable gives Joseph's request first and then explains who he was in short sentences, and says that Arimathea was a town.

source.text: ἦλθεν οὖν καὶ ἦρεν τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: Came therefore and took away the body of him.

en.L: So he came and took away {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} body.
en.B: So Joseph came and took {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} body away.
en.R: So Joseph came and took Jesus's body away.

decisions.choice: he came and took away (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus, have the plural, "they came and took away his body", perhaps because Nicodemus is named in the next verse and verse 40 says "they". The SBLGNT has the singular, and the sense is the same: Joseph saw that the body was removed, and others helped (verses 39-40). A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: took away his body: took it down from the cross
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in verses 31 and 38: the body is removed from the cross. John does not say who did the lifting down.

decisions.choice: Joseph (B, R); Jesus's body (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Joseph, since the last person named in the sentence before is Pilate. Readable also names Jesus for "his".

source.text: ἦλθεν δὲ καὶ Νικόδημος, ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτὸς τὸ πρῶτον, φέρων μίγμα σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης ὡς λίτρας ἑκατόν.

records.literal_gloss: Came and also Nicodemus, the [one] having come to him by night the first [time], bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes about litras a hundred.

en.L: And Nicodemus also came, the one who had first come to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about 100 pounds.
en.B: Nicodemus came too, the man who had first come to Jesus at night. He brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing {{units:about 70 pounds|about 100 Roman pounds}}.
en.R: Nicodemus came too. He was the man who had come to see Jesus one night some time before. He brought {{units:about 70 pounds|about 100 Roman pounds}} of spices, myrrh mixed with aloes.

decisions.choice: Nicodemus: the Pharisee and ruler who came to Jesus by night
decisions.reason: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night in 3:1-2, and spoke up for a fair hearing for him in the council (7:50-51). Now, with Joseph, he honors Jesus openly. John recalls the night visit here, as he did at 3:2; for what "night" may suggest, see the note there.

decisions.choice: at first: the first time, earlier in the story
decisions.reason: The phrase looks back to his first coming to Jesus, in chapter 3, not to the order in which the two men came to the cross. Joseph has just been named.

decisions.choice: myrrh and aloes: fragrant spices for honoring the dead
decisions.reason: Myrrh is a sweet-smelling resin from a shrub of Arabia and East Africa (Matthew 2:11). The aloes are most likely the fragrant wood of an eastern tree, powdered, not the plant used for medicine; myrrh and aloes are named together as perfumes in Psalm 45:9, Proverbs 7:17 and Song of Songs 4:14. They were laid with the body in the cloths (verse 40) to honor it and to mask the smell of death, not to embalm it as the Egyptians did.

decisions.choice: about a hundred pounds: a hundred Roman pounds, about 33 kilograms (about 72 pounds)
decisions.reason: The unit is the Roman pound of about 327 grams, lighter than the modern pound; it is the measure of Mary's perfume at 12:3. A hundred of them is a very great weight of spices.

decisions.choice: a burial fit for a king
alternatives: simply a generous gift, with no further meaning
decisions.reason: Spices in great amounts were used for honored and royal burials (2 Chronicles 16:14; Jeremiah 34:5). After the title "King of the Jews" on the cross (19:19-22), the size of the gift may show that Jesus is buried as a king. John does not say so, and the amount may simply show the love and wealth of the giver.

decisions.choice: {{units:about 70 pounds|about 100 Roman pounds}}
decisions.reason: A modern reader takes "a pound" as 16 ounces, so Balanced and Readable give the weight in modern pounds by default, rounded, and the units setting shows the Roman pounds, as at 12:3. Literal keeps the ancient unit. US units are the default; metric belongs to a future setting.

decisions.choice: Jesus (for "him"); some time before (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus. Readable says "some time before" for "at first" (meaning decision m2) and makes the description its own sentence.

source.text: ἔλαβον οὖν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἔδησαν αὐτὸ ὀθονίοις μετὰ τῶν ἀρωμάτων, καθὼς ἔθος ἐστὶν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ἐνταφιάζειν.

records.literal_gloss: They took therefore the body of the Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as custom is to the Jews to prepare for burial.

en.L: So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as [it] is [the] custom for the Jews to prepare for burial.
en.B: They took Jesus's body and wrapped it with the spices in linen cloths, which is how the Jews prepare a body for burial.
en.R: Joseph and Nicodemus took the body of Jesus. They wrapped it in pieces of linen cloth with the spices. This was the way the Jews got a body ready to be buried.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people and their customs
decisions.reason: Here the word names the people whose burial customs these were, as "the Passover of the Jews" names their feast (2:13; 11:55). Joseph and Nicodemus, who do this, are Jews.

decisions.choice: linen cloths: pieces of linen, of a size not stated
decisions.reason: The word is a small form of the word for linen cloth. The other Gospels speak of a linen sheet in which Joseph wrapped the body (Mark 15:46), and John uses this word again for the cloths left in the empty tomb (20:5-7). It may cover strips, sheets, or both; the text does not say.

decisions.choice: as is the custom of the Jews to prepare for burial: wrapping the body with spices, not embalming it
decisions.reason: Jewish custom was to wash the body, lay it out with spices or perfumed oil, and wrap it in cloths, then to bury it on the day of death. The body was not opened or embalmed, as was done in Egypt (Genesis 50:2-3). The verb for preparing for burial is related to the noun Jesus used when Mary anointed him (12:7).

decisions.choice: Joseph and Nicodemus
decisions.reason: Readable names the two men who have just been introduced (verses 38-39).

decisions.choice: wrapped (B, R); pieces of linen cloth (R); the Jews (all levels)
decisions.reason: "Bound" sounds like tying up; Balanced and Readable say "wrapped". "The Jews" here means the people (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps the word John wrote, with no footnote.

source.text: ἦν δὲ ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ὅπου ἐσταυρώθη κῆπος, καὶ ἐν τῷ κήπῳ μνημεῖον καινόν, ἐν ᾧ οὐδέπω οὐδεὶς ἦν τεθειμένος·

records.literal_gloss: Was now in the place where he was crucified a garden, and in the garden a tomb new, in which not yet no one had been laid;

en.L: Now in the place where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid;
en.B: There was a garden at the place where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had been crucified, and in that garden there was a new tomb where no one had ever been laid.
en.R: At the place where Jesus had been crucified there was a garden. In the garden there was a new tomb. No one had ever been buried in it.

decisions.choice: in the place where he was crucified: in the area of the crucifixion, close to it
alternatives: on the very spot of the cross
decisions.reason: "Place" is the site, the area around Golgotha, which was near the city (19:17, 20). The garden lay close by, and verse 42 says the tomb was near.

decisions.choice: a garden: the story that began in a garden ends in one
alternatives: no echo; only a note of place
an echo of the garden of Eden
decisions.reason: Only John says that the tomb was in a garden. Jesus was arrested in a garden (18:1, 26), is buried in one, and is taken for the gardener on the morning of the resurrection (20:15). Some readers also hear an echo of Eden and a new creation. John does not draw out either link.

decisions.choice: a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid: unused, and so fit to honor him
decisions.reason: Tombs near Jerusalem were often cut into the rock and used by a family for many burials over the years. This one had never been used. The other Gospels say it was Joseph's own new tomb cut in the rock (Matthew 27:60; Luke 23:53). The double negative in the Greek ("not yet no one") is emphatic: no one at all had ever been laid there.

decisions.choice: had been crucified; no one had ever been laid (B); buried (R); Jesus (R)
alternatives: no one had yet been laid (Literal)
decisions.reason: "Ever" gives the force of the emphatic double negative (meaning decision m3). Readable says "buried" for "laid", names Jesus for "he", and uses three short sentences.

source.text: ἐκεῖ οὖν διὰ τὴν παρασκευὴν τῶν Ἰουδαίων, ὅτι ἐγγὺς ἦν τὸ μνημεῖον, ἔθηκαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν.

records.literal_gloss: There therefore because of the Preparation of the Jews, because near was the tomb, they laid the Jesus.

en.L: So there, because of the Preparation of the Jews, since the tomb was near, they laid Jesus.
en.B: The tomb was close at hand, and it was the Jewish day of Preparation, so they laid Jesus there.
en.R: It was the Jewish day of Preparation, and the Sabbath would soon begin. The tomb was close by, so they laid Jesus there.

decisions.choice: the Preparation of the Jews: the day in the Jewish calendar
decisions.reason: The phrase names the day by the people who kept it, as John speaks of "the Passover of the Jews" (2:13; 11:55) and "the festival of the Jews" (5:1; 7:2). It does not refer to the authorities.

decisions.choice: because of the Preparation: the Sabbath was about to begin
decisions.reason: The Sabbath began at sunset (verse 31), and no burial work could be done once it had begun. The women return to the tomb only when the Sabbath is over (20:1; Luke 23:54-56).

decisions.choice: two reasons: the day, and the tomb being near
alternatives: a burial meant to be only for the time being
decisions.reason: The shortness of the time and the nearness of the tomb explain why Jesus was laid there. John does not say whether the burial was meant to be temporary; the full preparation of the body (verses 39-40) suggests it was not hurried in its care. "There" comes first in the Greek and "Jesus" last, so the chapter ends with the place where he lies, the setting of chapter 20.

decisions.choice: the Jewish day of Preparation
decisions.reason: Here "the Jews" means the people (meaning decision m1), so Balanced and Readable say "Jewish", as at 11:55 ("the Jewish Passover"); no footnote is needed.

decisions.choice: and the Sabbath would soon begin
decisions.reason: Readable says why the day of Preparation mattered (meaning decision m2), which verse 31 has already told.
